title: Photoshop or Illustrator: which one you actually need, by task
excerpt: Pixels or paths. A task-by-task guide to choosing between Photoshop and Illustrator, the four mistakes that cost the most time, and which to learn first.
body_html:
The question comes up in almost every beginner class, usually after somebody has spent an afternoon fighting the wrong application. Photoshop and Illustrator both sit in the same subscription, both open with a blank canvas, and both can put a red circle on the screen. They are not interchangeable, and choosing the wrong one costs you time at the start and quality at the end.

The difference is simple to state and easy to forget once you are inside the software. Photoshop edits pixels. Illustrator draws shapes described by maths. A Photoshop file is a grid of coloured squares at a fixed resolution, so it has a size beyond which it starts to fall apart. An Illustrator file is a set of instructions: this curve, this thickness, this fill. Those instructions can be redrawn at any size, from a favicon to the side of a bus, with no loss at all.

Choose by the task, not by the tool you already know

Here is the practical version. Look for your job in this list and use the application next to it.

Use Photoshop for

  • Photographs. Retouching skin, removing an object from a background, correcting exposure and colour, and any work where the source is a camera file.
  • Compositing. Putting three photographs into one scene so it reads as a single image, with masks, shadows and matching colour.
  • Mock-ups and visualisations. Showing a design on a shopfront, a T-shirt or a phone screen.
  • Web and social imagery. Banners, thumbnails and any graphic that will only ever be viewed on a screen at a known size.
  • Textures and painted artwork. Anything with brushwork, grain or photographic detail.

Use Illustrator for

  • Logos. Every logo should exist as vector artwork. A client will eventually ask for it on a pull-up banner, embroidered on a shirt and 16 pixels wide in a browser tab. One file has to serve all three.
  • Icons and pictograms. Sets that must stay consistent in weight and shape at several sizes.
  • Illustration with clean edges. Flat character work, technical drawing, maps, diagrams and infographics.
  • Packaging and labels. Anything drawn to a printer's dieline, where the cut path and the artwork must line up exactly.
  • Type as artwork. Wordmarks, lettering and type that will be stretched, outlined or cut in vinyl.
  • Spot colours and screen printing. Work that has to separate cleanly into named inks.

The tests that settle an argument

When a job sits on the boundary, three questions decide it.

Does the artwork need to survive being resized? If the answer is yes, and you cannot name the final size today, it is vector work and it belongs in Illustrator. A logo drawn in Photoshop at 2,000 pixels wide looks perfect until a signage company asks for it two metres across, and then it cannot be rescued without redrawing it.

Is the source material a photograph? Photographs are pixels by nature. There is no vector version of a face. Anything that starts in a camera is edited in Photoshop, or in Lightroom before it reaches Photoshop.

Does a printer need paths? Cutting, foiling, embossing and engraving all need a line the machine can follow. Those lines are vector paths, which means Illustrator.

Where the two work together

Most real jobs use both, in sequence. A common pattern for a product poster looks like this. The photograph is corrected and cut out in Photoshop and saved as a layered PSD. The logo and any diagrams are drawn in Illustrator. The two are placed into InDesign, which handles the page, the type and the export to a print-ready PDF. Nothing is copied and flattened, so when the client changes the price on the poster you change one text frame rather than rebuilding the artwork.

Photoshop and Illustrator also pass work between them directly. You can place an Illustrator file into Photoshop as a smart object, which keeps it sharp when you scale it inside the mock-up. You can copy a path out of Illustrator and use it as a clipping path in Photoshop. Learning those handovers matters more than mastering either application in isolation.

Four mistakes that cost the most time

Building a logo in Photoshop. This is the expensive one. The client is happy, the file goes out, and six months later the brand needs a vector version for a supplier. Somebody has to trace it by hand, and the traced version never quite matches. Draw it in Illustrator on day one.

Enlarging a JPEG and hoping. Upscaling adds pixels the camera never captured. Modern upscaling is better than it was, and for a photograph it can be good enough, but it will not turn a soft logo into a crisp one.

Retouching in Illustrator. Illustrator can hold a photograph, but it cannot edit one in any meaningful way. Effects applied to a placed image in Illustrator are also a frequent cause of print files that will not process.

Laying out multi-page documents in either. A brochure, a report or a catalogue belongs in InDesign. Photoshop and Illustrator have no master pages, no automatic page numbering and no text flow across pages, so a twelve-page document built in them becomes twelve separate problems.

What comes out of each

The export step is where the difference becomes visible to everyone else. From Illustrator you hand over AI as the working file, SVG for the web, EPS when an old print workflow asks for it, and PDF for almost everything else. From Photoshop you hand over PSD as the working file, TIFF or a press-ready PDF for print, and PNG or JPEG for screen. If a supplier asks for "the vector", they are asking for artwork that came out of Illustrator, and a PNG will not do.

Which should you learn first?

It depends on the work in front of you rather than on which is easier.

Learn Photoshop first if you are handling photography, running social media, producing web imagery, or working anywhere that images arrive from a camera and have to be made presentable. It is also the more transferable first step if you are not yet sure what kind of design work you want.

Learn Illustrator first if you are heading towards branding, packaging, apparel, signage or illustration, or if you already have clients asking you for a logo. The drawing tools take longer to feel natural, so starting earlier helps.

If you are aiming at a full graphic design role, you will need all three of Photoshop, Illustrator and InDesign, and studios in Colombo generally expect that in a portfolio rather than depth in only one. Learning them in that order, with a project that carries through all three, is far more useful than three unconnected tutorials.

A note on certification

Both applications have their own Adobe Certified Professional exam, delivered through Certiport. The exams are separate, so passing the Photoshop exam says nothing about your Illustrator ability, and vice versa. If you complete two related professional certifications you can earn an Adobe Specialty Credential, such as Visual Design. That is worth knowing before you decide which exam to sit first: pick the one that matches the work you are actually doing, then add the second.

If you already use Photoshop and keep hitting its limits on logos, icons and print artwork, Illustrator is the gap. Our Illustrator Level 1 course starts from the pen tool and finishes with a logo delivered in the formats a printer and a web developer will each accept.
